prompt: If $\dfrac{2x - 1}{5} = \dfrac{x + 4}{3}$, what is the value of $x$?
hint: A single fraction equals a single fraction here. What technique removes both denominators in one move?

hints.text: A single fraction equals a single fraction here. What technique removes both denominators in one move?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try a simpler proportion: $\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{6}{3}$. Cross-multiply to get $3x = 12$, so $x = 4$. Cross-multiplying works identically when the numerators are expressions instead of single letters.
Cross-multiply to get $3(2x - 1) = 5(x + 4)$. Distribute on both sides, taking care with the $-1$, and then collect terms.
Distributing gives $6x - 3 = 5x + 20$. Subtracting $5x$ and adding $3$ leaves the answer $x = 23$.

learningObjective: Solve a proportion involving linear expressions.
explanation: Cross-multiply, which is the same as multiplying both sides by $15$ to clear the denominators: $3(2x - 1) = 5(x + 4)$.
Distribute on each side so the brackets disappear: $6x - 3 = 5x + 20$.
Subtract $5x$ from both sides and add $3$ to both sides, which leaves $x = 23$.
Check both fractions: $\dfrac{45}{5} = 9$ and $\dfrac{27}{3} = 9$, so the value of $x$ is $23$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Multiply by the common denominator
steps: The denominators are $5$ and $3$, so multiply every term by $15$.
The left becomes $3(2x - 1)$ and the right becomes $5(x + 4)$ — exactly the cross-multiplied form.
Cross-multiplication is not a separate trick; it is this step with the arithmetic already done.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Cross-multiplying only one way — writing 3(2x − 1) = x + 4 — forgets the 5 and lands on a tidy wrong x.
In a cross-multiplication BOTH numerators pick up the opposite denominator. Draw the two diagonal arrows before writing anything.
